---
title: "Exercises — Nucleic acids as a building material"
---

Pen and paper. Try each one before opening the **Hint**, and the hint before the
**Solution** — the reasoning is the point, not the answer.

Have the [NEB selection charts](https://www.neb.com/en/tools-and-resources/selection-charts)
open for the enzyme questions.

# Part 1 — End states

## E1. Why does end repair exist?

You have sheared human genomic DNA with a Covaris to around 350 bp. You want to ligate a
double-stranded adapter with a single 3' T overhang to both ends of every fragment.

List everything about the sheared ends that would stop that ligation working, and the
operation that fixes each one.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Shearing breaks the backbone mechanically. It does not care about producing a chemically
tidy end. Think about the four things a ligase needs: the right shape, a 5'-phosphate, a free
3'-OH, and the overhang it expects.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
| Problem at the end | Fix |
|---|---|
| Ragged ends: a mixture of blunt, 5' and 3' overhangs | Fill in 5' overhangs, chew back 3' overhangs → blunt |
| Some 5' ends have no phosphate | T4 polynucleotide kinase adds one |
| Some 3' ends are damaged or phosphorylated, so nothing can extend or ligate | T4 PNK's 3' phosphatase activity; damaged ends are removed by the chew-back |
| Blunt ends do not match the adapter's T overhang | Add a single non-templated A to each 3' end (dA-tailing) |

"End repair" in a kit is the first three happening in one tube; A-tailing is usually a
separate step or a separate enzyme mix because it needs a polymerase that will *not* remove
the A again.
:::

## E2. The A-tail trap

A-tailing is done with Klenow fragment **exo−**, not with ordinary Klenow or with a
high-fidelity proofreading polymerase. Why not? What would happen if you used a proofreading
enzyme, and would you see an error message?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Look up the 3'→5' exonuclease column for each enzyme. What is an unpaired A at a 3' end, as
far as a proofreading polymerase is concerned?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
A proofreading polymerase's 3'→5' exonuclease exists to remove unpaired 3' terminal
nucleotides. The non-templated A is exactly that: unpaired. The enzyme would add it and
remove it in a futile cycle, leaving you with blunt ends.

There is no error message. The reaction looks normal, the DNA is intact, and you only find
out at the next step: adapter ligation is very inefficient, and the library yield is low or
dominated by adapter dimers.

This is the general shape of the most dangerous failures in library prep — an activity you
did not want, acting on a substrate you did not think about.
:::

## E3. Nicks, gaps and who repairs them

For each situation, say whether a ligase alone is enough, and if not what must happen first:

a. A double-stranded molecule where one strand's backbone is cut between two adjacent bases
b. The product of Tn5 tagmentation, which leaves a 9 nt single-stranded region on each side
c. Two blunt fragments you want to join end to end
d. A duplex where one strand is missing its 5'-phosphate at the cut

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Ask in each case: are any *bases* missing, and does each side present the right chemistry?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. A nick: nothing is missing, so a ligase seals it directly.
b. A gap, not a nick: 9 bases are absent. A polymerase must fill in first (this is the
   "gap fill" step after tagmentation), then a ligase — or the first PCR cycle does it.
c. A ligase can do it, but blunt ligation is slow and unselective. This is why protocols add
   overhangs when they can.
d. Nothing happens. T4 PNK must add the phosphate first. Some protocols leave the phosphate
   off deliberately so that only one of the two strands is joined.
:::

# Part 2 — Hybridisation

## E4. Designing a poly(A) capture

You are capturing mRNA from total human RNA on oligo-dT beads.

a. Why is the binding step done in high salt, and the elution in water or low-salt buffer at
   an elevated temperature?
b. A colleague's capture recovers almost nothing. Their only deviation: they washed the beads
   with a buffer at 50 °C instead of room temperature. What happened?
c. Why is the dT stretch typically 20–25 nt rather than 8 nt?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
An oligo-dT:poly(A) duplex is made entirely of A–T pairs, with two hydrogen bonds each. What
does that do to its Tm compared with a mixed-sequence duplex of the same length? What does
salt do to two molecules that are both negatively charged?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Tm belongs to a duplex *in a buffer*, and salt is one of the levers that raises it: it
   shields the negative charge on both backbones and lets them approach, so binding is done in
   high salt. Taking the salt away and warming pushes the same duplex the other way, past its
   Tm — which is the elution.
b. Only the temperature changed, and this is the weakest duplex anywhere in the protocol:
   every pair is A–T, with two hydrogen bonds and no G or C to push the Tm up, so it is the
   first thing in the tube to open when the beads are warmed. At 50 °C the wash was above its
   Tm, the mRNA came off into the wash, and the wash went down the drain. There is no way to
   tell this apart from "capture failed" without having measured.
c. An AT-only duplex is weak per base pair, so length is the only lever left once the sequence
   is fixed: it needs 20–25 bases to hold at working temperatures. An 8-mer dT would not hold
   at room temperature, and it would also bind any short A-rich stretch anywhere in a
   transcript.

This is the adapter-stem calculation from the walk with the aim reversed: there the duplex has
to stay shut through a ligation at room temperature, here it has to be opened on purpose, and
the same three levers — length, GC, salt — do both jobs.
:::

## E5. Reading a fragment-analyser trace

Your library trace shows the expected broad peak around 320 bp, and a second sharp peak at
about 130 bp that is nearly as tall.

a. What is the 130 bp peak almost certainly?
b. Why is it dangerous to load this library as it is, even though most of the material is the
   right size?
c. Give two ways to prevent it next time, and one way to rescue this library now.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
What is the length of two adapters joined to each other, with no insert in between? And what
does a sequencer prefer when it has a choice of fragment lengths?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Adapter dimers: two adapters ligated directly to each other.
b. Short molecules cluster and amplify more efficiently than long ones, so dimers are
   over-represented on the flow cell relative to their share of the trace. They produce
   reads containing only adapter, which are worthless. A dimer peak of this size can consume
   a large fraction of the run.
c. Prevention: a single A on the insert and a single T on the adapter, so that an adapter end
   can only pair with an insert end and not with another adapter; and adapter concentration
   matched to the amount of input DNA, since the more adapter ends there are per insert end,
   the more often two adapters meet each other first. Rescue: a size selection — a bead
   clean-up at a ratio that leaves short fragments in solution, or a gel cut.
:::

# Part 3 — Oligo design

## E6. Which strand does it anneal to?

An adapter's top strand ends `...AGATCGGAAGAGC`. You design a primer `GCTCTTCCGATCT`.

a. What is the relationship between the two sequences?
b. Which strand will your primer anneal to, and in which direction will it extend?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Write the second sequence out and reverse it, then complement each base. Remember both are
written 5'→3' by convention.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. `GCTCTTCCGATCT` is the reverse complement of `AGATCGGAAGAGC`.
b. It anneals to the strand that *contains* `AGATCGGAAGAGC`, and extends away from that
   adapter, across the insert — it reads into the insert, which is what a sequencing or
   amplification primer for this adapter must do.

Working this out by hand for every oligo in a protocol is tedious but it is the only way to
be certain. The *Annotate sequence* tool on the NGS 101 site does it for you once you trust
your own reasoning.
:::

## E7. Degenerate positions

a. You want an 8 nt UMI in a primer — a random stretch that tags one starting molecule, so
   that two reads carrying the same tag can be recognised as copies of it. How do you specify
   that stretch when ordering, and how many distinct molecules does it produce?
b. Oligo-dT primers are often ordered as `T(20)VN` rather than `T(22)`. What does `VN` mean,
   and what problem does it solve?
c. Why can a UMI never be added during PCR?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
For (b), think about where along a poly(A) tail of 150 A's an oligo-dT primer would otherwise
anneal, and where you would like it to sit.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Eight `N` positions: the synthesiser uses a mixture of all four bases at each, giving
   4⁸ = 65,536 distinct sequences in one tube.
b. `V` is A, C or G — anything but T. `N` is any base. The two positions sit at the very
   junction between the poly(A) tail and the transcript body, so the primer anchors at the
   start of the tail instead of annealing somewhere in the middle of it. Without the anchor
   you lose a variable and unknown amount of the 3' end of each transcript.
c. A UMI must mark a molecule *before* it is copied. Anything introduced during amplification
   labels copies, not originals, so it cannot distinguish a PCR duplicate from a second real
   molecule. UMIs are added by ligation, in an RT primer, or in a template-switch oligo.
:::

## E8. Specifying an oligo for a job

For each requirement, name the modification you would order and say what it does:

a. A capture oligo that must be pulled down on streptavidin beads
b. A blocking oligo that must hybridise but must never be extended by a polymerase
c. A primer that must survive an exonuclease treatment that removes everything else
d. An adapter that must be cut out again later, at a defined position, without a restriction
   enzyme
e. A 5' end that a ligase will accept as the donor

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. 5' or 3' **biotin** — binds streptavidin essentially irreversibly.
b. A **3' blocking group**: C3 spacer, dideoxy C, or an inverted dT. No free 3'-OH, so no
   extension.
c. **Phosphorothioate** linkages at the terminal few positions — the sulfur substitution makes
   the bond a poor substrate for exonucleases.
d. One or more **dU** bases: UDG removes the uracil and an AP endonuclease breaks the backbone
   there (together sold as USER). The cut position is wherever you put the U.
e. A **5' phosphate**. Order it explicitly; synthetic oligos come with a 5'-OH by default.
:::

## E9. Ordering and stock solutions

a. You receive an oligo as a dried pellet of 25 nmol. How much nuclease-free water do you add
   for a 100 µM stock?
b. Why are long adapters often ordered as two shorter oligos that you anneal yourself, rather
   than as one long oligo?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
For (a): 100 µM is 100 nmol/mL. For (b): synthesis adds one base at a time, and each coupling
is slightly less than perfect.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. 250 µL. 25 nmol / 0.25 mL = 100 nmol/mL = 100 µM.
b. At ~99% coupling efficiency per base, the fraction of full-length product falls
   exponentially with length: a 60-mer is only about 0.99⁵⁹ ≈ 55% full length. The truncated
   molecules are not inert — a shortened adapter still ligates, but produces a library
   molecule missing part of a primer site, which never amplifies or never sequences. Two
   30-mers annealed together are each far purer, and the annealing step itself selects for
   molecules that can pair.
:::

# Part 4 — RNA

## E10. Fragmented RNA will not ligate

You fragment total RNA by heating it with magnesium, then try to ligate a pre-adenylated
3' adapter. Nothing happens. You also plan a 5' adapter ligation later.

a. What ends does metal-ion or alkaline fragmentation leave?
b. Which enzyme fixes them, and which two activities of it do you need?
c. Why does the order of operations matter here?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
RNA's 2'-OH attacks its own backbone. Think about what that leaves behind on each side of the
break, and compare it with what an RNA ligase requires at each end.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. A 2',3'-cyclic phosphate on one side and a 5'-OH on the other — the opposite of what is
   needed at both ends.
b. T4 polynucleotide kinase. Its **3' phosphatase** activity opens and removes the cyclic
   phosphate, leaving 3'-OH; its **kinase** activity adds a 5'-phosphate. Note that the
   "3' phosphatase minus" variant of PNK will not do the first job.
c. The 3' adapter ligation needs a free 3'-OH on the RNA, and the 5' adapter ligation needs a
   5'-phosphate on the RNA. If you phosphorylate everything first and then ligate the 3'
   adapter, you must make sure the adapter's own ends cannot take part — which is why 3'
   adapters are supplied pre-adenylated and 3'-blocked, so they can only act as the donor and
   cannot self-ligate.
:::

# Part 5 — Choosing the enzyme

## E11. Reading the polymerase chart

Using the NEB DNA polymerase selection chart, pick an enzyme for each job and name the column
that decides it:

a. Fill in a 5' overhang, without displacing the strand downstream of it
b. Amplify a bisulfite-converted template, in which most cytosines are now uracil
c. Amplify a 12 kb product with as few errors as possible
d. Copy a circular template round and round, displacing the strand ahead
e. Add a single non-templated A to a blunt 3' end

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
The deciding columns are, in order: strand displacement; dU tolerance; fidelity and maximum
product length; strand displacement again; resulting 3' ends together with 3'→5' exonuclease.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. **T4 DNA polymerase** — no strand displacement, and its 3'→5' exonuclease also trims 3'
   overhangs, which is why it is the end-repair enzyme. Klenow would work but can displace.
b. A **uracil-tolerant** polymerase. Archaeal proofreading enzymes read ahead and stall at
   uracil, and bisulfite conversion creates a great many uracils; the chart's dU tolerance
   column is the one that matters.
c. A **high-fidelity** polymerase with a long maximum product: fidelity and max PCR product
   columns together.
d. **phi29** — strong strand displacement and high processivity, which is what makes rolling
   circle amplification and MDA possible.
e. **Klenow exo−** — the resulting 3' ends column says +A, and exo− means the A is not removed
   again (see E2).
:::

## E12. The activity you did not want

Each of these is a real failure mode. Name the unwanted enzyme activity:

a. A nick you created deliberately, to mark one strand, has vanished and the strand beyond it
   has been replaced
b. Your 3'-blocked blocking oligo has been shortened and now primes
c. Your carefully made 3' overhangs are blunt before you ligate
d. Your uracil-containing adapter is destroyed during PCR

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. **5'→3' exonuclease / flap endonuclease** — nick translation. Pol I and Taq do this;
   Klenow and T4 DNA polymerase do not.
b. **3'→5' exonuclease** on a proofreading polymerase, chewing in from the 3' end until it
   passes the block.
c. **3'→5' exonuclease** again, this time doing the job it is famous for.
d. Not an exonuclease at all — **uracil excision** by a contaminating or deliberately added
   UDG, or a polymerase that stalls at U so the adapter is never copied at all. Check whether
   your master mix contains UDG, which some kits include to prevent carry-over contamination.
:::

# Self-check

Answer without looking anything up.

1. Which end of a strand can a polymerase extend?
2. A ligase joins two molecules. What must be present on each side?
3. What is the difference between a nick and a gap?
4. Which raises Tm: more GC, or more salt? (Trick question.)
5. Why can a UMI not be introduced during PCR?
6. What does a 3' C3 spacer do?
7. What ends does alkaline fragmentation of RNA leave?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. The 3' end — always, with no exceptions among the enzymes in this course.
2. A 5'-phosphate on the donor side and a free 3'-OH on the acceptor side.
3. A nick is a cut backbone with all bases present; a gap has bases missing. A ligase can
   seal a nick but not a gap.
4. Both do. It was a trick question: Tm depends on sequence *and* on the buffer.
5. Because it would label copies rather than original molecules, which is precisely the
   distinction it exists to make.
6. Blocks the 3' end so no polymerase can extend it and no ligase can use it as the acceptor.
7. A 2',3'-cyclic phosphate and a 5'-OH.
:::
